title: Reproducible determination of transpulmonary pressures
author: De Meyer, Morrison, et al.

steps.title: Trim data to experiment window
steps.instruction: Delete every row in the raw data file that was recorded before the recorded start time of the experiment or after the recorded end time.

steps.title: Select end‑expiratory breaths
steps.instruction:
Filter the remaining rows to keep only end‑expiratory points that satisfy both of the following criteria:
1. Airway pressure is within ±1 cmH₂O of the set PEEP (e.g., for a set PEEP of 15 cmH₂O keep pressures between 14 and 16 cmH₂O).
2. Flow is within ±10 L/min of zero (to allow for recording noise).

steps.title: Exclude outlier transpulmonary pressures
steps.instruction: From the column of end‑expiratory transpulmonary pressures, remove any values that are outliers according to Tukey’s rule: values smaller than Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or larger than Q3 + 1.5 × IQR are discarded. (Other outlier‑detection methods may be used, but Tukey’s rule is the default.)

steps.title: Compute median end‑expiratory pressure
steps.instruction: Calculate the median of the remaining end‑expiratory transpulmonary pressure values; this median is the representative end‑expiratory transpulmonary pressure (PLee).

steps.title: Run the R data‑processing script
steps.instruction:
Use the provided purpose‑built R script (compatible with FluxMed GrT or BIOPAC MP36R recordings) as follows:
1. Place all raw data files in a single directory.
2. Supply the set PEEP levels (high = 15 cmH₂O, medium = 10 cmH₂O, low = 5 cmH₂O) as input arguments.
3. The script automatically applies steps 1‑4, removing rows outside set PEEP ± 1 cmH₂O.
4. The script outputs a table with three columns: ID, set PEEP, and median PLee (the median end‑expiratory transpulmonary pressure for that PEEP).

description: The standard clinical practice of visually inspecting transpulmonary pressure-time plots, PL(t), is labour intensive and therefore limits the amount of data points that can be used to calculate a representative mean or median transpulmonary pressure during the period of interest. Additionally, this method is prone to inter-observer bias. However, this approach has the advantage that a trained clinician can judge the quality of the recording while only taking samples at representative points and ignoring, for instance, the effects of oesophageal contractions or patient manipulation. We designed a method of data extraction, using all representative data points, with the aim of improving reproducibility (Fig. 3).Fig. 3Graphical illustration of calculated median end-expiratory transpulmonary pressure (red line) in reference to the raw transpulmonary pressure (PL) - time wave. cmH2O: centimetres of water pressure; PLee: end-expiratory transpulmonary pressure; s: seconds.Fig 3 We identified four important steps to obtain the representative end-expiratory transpulmonary pressure from the raw data recording.1.Remove all data points recorded before the start or after the end of the experiment.2.Filter for end-expiratory values only. At end-expiration:a.the recorded airway pressures should be close to the set positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP).We used a margin of ±1 cmH2O around set PEEP. For example, if PEEP was set at 15 cmH2O, the airway pressures in the raw data were filtered for values between 14 and 16 cmH2O to account for variation in the measurement.b.the recorded flow should approximately be zero.For the flow, we used a margin of ±10 L/min around zero as some noise on the recording may be present.3.Remove all non-sense data points from the end-expiratory transpulmonary pressure column.
